'''Patrick Ximenes Gallagher''' (January 2, 1935<ref name="AMWS">{{cite book|title=[[American Men and Women of Science]] |publisher=[[Gale (publisher)|Gale]] |edition=21st |volume=3 |year=2004 |page=16 |quote=GALLAGHER, PATRICK XIMENES. Personal Data: b Elizabeth. NJ. January 2, 1935. Education: Harvard Univ, AB, 1956; Princeton Univ, PhD(math), 1959. Professional Experience: PROF MATH, COLUMBIA UNIV. 1972-; from assoc prof to prof math, Bar nard Col, 1965-1972; mem, Inst Advan Study, 1964-1965; asst prof, Columbia Univ, 1962-1964; Instr, Mass Inst Technol, 1959-1961; Asst math, Princeton Univ, 1957-1959. Memberships: Am Math Soc. Mailing Address: Dept Math, Columbia Univ 299 Broadway 517 Math MC 4439, New York, NY 10027-6902.}}</ref><ref name="mem-flyer">{{cite web |url=http://www.math.columbia.edu/~staff/GallagherMemorialS.pdf |title=In memory of Patrick X. Gallagher |publisher=[[Columbia University]] |access-date=August 4, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191222125808/http://math.columbia.edu/~staff/GallagherMemorialS.pdf |archive-date=December 22, 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref> – March 30, 2019)<ref name="mem-flyer"/><ref name="mem-conf">{{cite web|url=http://www.math.columbia.edu/2019/08/21/memorial-conference-for-patrick-ximenes-gallagher/ |publisher=Columbia University |title=Memorial Conference for Patrick Ximenes Gallagher |date=August 21, 2019 |access-date=August 26, 2019}}</ref> was an American mathematician who pioneered [[large sieve|large sieve theory]] and invented the [[larger sieve]].

==Biography==
===Early life===
Patrick Ximenes Gallagher was born on January 2, 1935, in [[Elizabeth, New Jersey|Elizabeth]], [[New Jersey]] to school superintendent Ralph P. Gallagher and elementary school teacher Natalie Forcheimer Gallagher.<ref name="AMWS"/><ref>{{cite news |publisher=[[Courier News]] |title=Natalie F. Gallagher, active in community |page=B-2  |date=February 4, 1995 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/222505863/ |access-date=December 28, 2019}}</ref><ref name="Courier1956"/> Gallagher graduated from [[Bound Brook High School]] and received a scholarship from the Harvard Club of New Jersey to attend [[Harvard University]].<ref name="Courier1956">{{cite news |publisher=[[Courier News]] |title=Gets Princeton Assistant Post |page=12 |date=June 16, 1956 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/221526064 |access-date=December 28, 2019}}</ref><ref name="HomeNews1956"/>

===Education===
In 1956, Gallagher received a B.A. degree ''magna cum laude'' from Harvard University.<ref name="IAS">{{cite web |title=Patrick X. Gallagher |publisher=Institute for Advanced Study |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/patrick-x-gallagher |access-date=8 February 2019}}</ref><ref name="Courier1956"/> At Harvard, he was a member of the Harvard Mathematics Club and [[Eliot House (Harvard College)|Eliot House]] Mathematics-Physics Club and completed an undergraduate honors thesis entitled ''On a property of some entire functions''.<ref name="HomeNews1956">{{cite news |publisher=[[Home News Tribune|The Central Jersey Home News]] |title=Bound Brook Man Awarded Assistantship At Princeton |page=8 |date=June 17, 1956 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/315455366 |access-date=December 28, 2019}}</ref> In 1959, Gallagher received a PhD from [[Princeton University]] with a doctoral dissertation entitled ''Metric Diophantine Approximation in One and Several Dimensions'' completed under the supervision of [[Donald C. Spencer]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy |id=29521}}</ref>

===Career===
After receiving his doctoral degree, Gallagher served as an instructor at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] from 1959 to 1961.<ref name="AMWS"/> He spent one year living in the [[Latin Quarter, Paris|Latin Quarter]] of Paris before becoming an assistant professor at [[Columbia University]] in 1962.<ref name="AMWS"/><ref name="eulogy">{{cite AV media |people=Andrew Gallagher |title=Eulogy Patrick X. Gallagher Columbia University 10/10/19 |date=October 10, 2019 |medium=Video |publisher=YouTube}}</ref> He moved from Columbia to become a member of the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] for the 1964-1965 academic year.<ref name="AMWS"/> From 1965 to 1972, he was an associate professor and then full professor at [[Barnard College]].<ref name="AMWS"/><ref name="IAS"/>

In 1972, Gallagher moved back to Columbia University as a professor of mathematics.<ref name="directory"/><ref name="DS"/><ref name="AMWS"/> Gallagher received the Columbia University Presidential Teaching Award in 2005<ref name="IAS"/> and became director of undergraduate studies in the department of mathematics in 2013.<ref name="directory">{{cite web |title=Patrick Gallagher |url=http://www.math.columbia.edu/people/faculty-by-rank/name/patrick-gallagher/ |publisher=Columbia University |access-date=8 February 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160621072042/http://www.math.columbia.edu/people/faculty-by-rank/name/patrick-gallagher/ |archive-date=June 21, 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="DS">{{cite web |first=Amber |last=Tunnell |title=Over Past 12 Years, Grade Inflation Increases |url=https://www.columbiaspectator.com/2008/12/01/over-past-12-years-grade-inflation-increases/ |publisher=Columbia Daily Spectator |date=March 27, 2013 |access-date=February 8, 2019}}</ref> He retired from Columbia in 2017 and was professor emeritus until his death in 2019.<ref name="mem-conf"/>

==Research==
In the 1960s and 1970s, Gallagher proved several results in [[large sieve|large sieve methods]] in [[analytic number theory]] and simplified key ingredients used in the proof of the [[Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem]].<ref>{{cite book |title=Introduction to Analytic and Probabilistic Number Theory | first=Gérald | last=Tenenbaum | series=Graduate Studies in Mathematics | volume=163 | publisher=American Mathematical Society | year=2015 | isbn=9780821898543  | pages=102–104 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Analytic Number Theory |first1 = Henryk |last1=Iwaniec |author-link1=Henryk Iwaniec |first2=Emmanuel |last2=Kowalski |publisher=American Mathematical Society |series=Colloquium Publications |volume=53 |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-8218-3633-0 |pages=183}}</ref> He also applied the large sieve to study the asymptotics of [[Galois group]]s of monic integral polynomials of bounded [[Glossary of arithmetic and diophantine geometry#N|height]], improving on results by [[Bartel Leendert van der Waerden|van der Waerden]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Gallagher |first=Patrick X. |editor-first=Harold G. |editor-last=Diamond |chapter=The large sieve and probabilistic Galois theory |title=Analytic number theory |series=Proceedings of Symposia in Pure Mathematics |volume=24 |pages= 91–101 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |year=1973}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The large sieve inequalities |last=Kowalski |first=Emmanuel |url=https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2007/08/08/emmanuel-kowalski-the-large-sieve-inequalities/ |date=August 8, 2007 |publisher=Terry Tao Wordpress |access-date=February 8, 2019}}</ref>

In 1971, he invented the [[larger sieve]].<ref>{{cite journal | first=Patrick | last=Gallagher | author-link=Patrick X. Gallagher | title=A larger sieve | journal=Acta Arithmetica  | volume=18 | year=1971 | pages=77–81 | doi=10.4064/aa-18-1-77-81 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Family==
Gallagher met his wife, Minh Chau Gallagher, while he was an instructor at MIT in 1960.<ref name="eulogy"/> Minh Chau was born in [[Hanoi]] to Roman Catholic parents.<ref>{{cite news|author=Sokolov, Raymond A.|newspaper=NY Times|title=She Learned How to Cook as a Girl in Hanoi|date=22 July 1971|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1971/07/22/archives/she-learned-how-to-cook-as-a-girl-in-hanoi.html|quote=Born in Hanoi of Roman Catholic parents, she attended Boston College and has been in the United States ever since.}}</ref> They had two sons together.<ref name="eulogy"/>
